glossary.text: A passport granted for a fixed donation or investment. The person becomes a full citizen, usually without living there.
The right to live in a country in exchange for an investment. It is not citizenship; a passport only comes later through normal naturalisation.
An umbrella label for residence-by-investment schemes. It is not one legal status and rules differ in every country.
Much of a CBI passport's value is visa-free travel (Schengen, UK). When a destination withdraws it, the passport loses value for every holder.

points.head: Two worlds
points.text: Passports for money are concentrated in small island states (the Caribbean five, Vanuatu, Nauru, São Tomé). Large economies sell residence, not citizenship.

points.head: Europe is closing, the Gulf and Latin America are opening
points.text: Spain, Ireland, the UK, Cyprus (CBI) and Malta (CBI) have closed since 2020. Every Gulf state now runs a long-term residence scheme, and Paraguay and Argentina are new entrants in 2026.

points.head: What this means for Blue Ocean
points.text: Client conversations should start from the goal (a passport, an EU base, a Gulf base, a tax home) and only then the country. A red or amber dot means do not sell it without a written check with the authority.

points.head: A passport can cost less than a residence permit
points.text: The cheapest passports (US$90,000–250,000) cost less than most European residence permits (€250,000–800,000). The difference is what the passport can do: weaker travel access and growing political risk.

points.head: Premium residence is a different market
points.text: Singapore, Hong Kong and New Zealand ask US$3–8 million and want active investment. They target family offices, not lifestyle buyers.

points.head: Entry price is not the full cost
points.text: Fees, due diligence, taxes and holding costs typically add 10–30% on top. Always quote the all-in figure to clients.

points.head: Property is still the main door
points.text: Property is the most common qualifying asset, but it mostly buys residence. Most passports are bought with a non-refundable donation.

points.head: Funds are replacing property in Europe
points.text: Portugal and Hungary moved from property to funds to cool housing markets. Expect the same shift elsewhere in the EU.

points.head: Boom, then backlash
points.text: 2012–2019 was the boom: Europe used golden visas to attract capital after the financial crisis. Since 2020 closures outnumber openings in Europe and Australia, driven by housing costs and security concerns.

points.head: The market is moving, not shrinking
points.text: Openings continue in the Gulf, Asia, Africa, the Pacific and Latin America. New programmes are smaller, cheaper or more selective.

points.head: The price war ended in 2024
points.text: Under pressure from the US and EU the five states agreed a US$200,000 floor; prices roughly doubled in a month.

points.head: Demand fell where the price rose most
points.text: St Kitts' CBI revenue fell from about 22% of GDP in 2023 to 8% in 2024 and about 5% in 2025 (IMF). These islands depend on the money, which is why the EU decision matters so much.

sources.title: Arton Capital, Caribbean price change 2024
IMF, St Kitts and Nevis 2025 Article IV

points.head: The value of a passport is set abroad
points.text: Each red cell was green a few years ago. When the UK, Ireland or the EU withdraws visa-free travel, every holder of that passport is affected, including people who bought it years ago.

points.head: The EU deadline is the key risk for 2027–2028
points.text: The EU asked all five Caribbean states to close their programmes by 1 June 2028; Antigua has proposed end-2030 and is still accepting applications. The Commission report due in December 2026 will show whether Schengen access is at risk.

points.head: Advice to clients
points.text: Do not present Caribbean CBI as a long-term Schengen solution. Present it as a travel document with political risk, and put EU residence options alongside it.

points.head: Closing the property route did not kill demand
points.text: Portugal issued more golden visas in 2023–2025 than in any year before, through funds, after property was removed.

points.head: Greece took Spain's place
points.text: Greek approvals nearly doubled in 2025 even after prices rose to €400,000–800,000, as Spain closed and processing sped up. New applications have since fallen.

points.head: Scale is very uneven
points.text: The Caribbean five have issued over 100,000 passports; premium Asian programmes grant a few hundred permits in a decade.
